Linear Algebra
Presented by: Sayali Mane

Linear Algebra is the mathematics of multidimensional data.
●
Scale: Handling billions of variables at once.
●
Efficiency: Finding the fastest path to a solution.
●
Prediction: Decoding patterns in chaotic markets.

Module 1: Vectors & Matrices
Industry: Gaming & VFX
Every character move or camera rotation in games like Call of Duty or Elden Ring is a matrix-vector multiplication.
The Math of Movement: P' = M · P Where P is the 3D vertex and M is the transformation matrix.

Why Matrices Drive Real Time Tech?
Hardware Speed : GPUs are built specifically to do matrix math. This is why Al and Games run so fast.
Cybersecurity : Matrices are used to encrypt and decrypt data in high-end cryptography.
Simulation : Architects use matrices to simulate how wind and earthquakes affect skyscrapers.

Module 2: Solving Linear Equations
Solving Ax=b
Industry: Supply Chain
Amazon and DHL solve massive systems of equations to decide which truck takes which route to minimize fuel and
time.
Solving Ax = b saves industries billions of dollars in "waste" energy and inventory costs.

Module 3: The Four Subspaces
Column Space : What is Possible
Column Space is the collection of all vectors that can be formed by combining the columns of a matrix. It shows all possible outputs of
the matrix.
Nullspace : What gets lost
Null Space is the collection of all vectors that become zero when multiplied by the matrix. It shows all inputs that produce no output.
Industry: Data Fitting

Importance: Managing Uncertainty
Error Correction : Space probes use "Nullspaces" to detect and fix data errors caused by cosmic radiation.
Reliability : Determining the Rank of a system tells engineers if their sensor data is redundant or unique.
Forecasting : Banks use subspaces to separate market "trends" (Column Space) from random "noise" (Nullspace).

Module 4: Eigenvalues/Vectors
An eigenvector is a special vector whose direction does not change after matrix multiplication, and the eigenvalue
tells us how much the vector is stretched or compressed.
Industry: Search Engines Google's PageRank algorithm treats the internet as a giant matrix.

The Math of Stability
Vibration Analysis Bridges have "natural frequencies" (Eigenvalues). Engineers must ensure wind doesn't hit those frequencies, or the
bridge will collapse.
Facial Recognition "Eigenfaces" are the core vectors used to identify humans by distilling faces into their most essential traits.

Module 5: The Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)
The Al Recommendation Secret Netflix doesn't know why you like a movie, but it uses SVD to find "Latent
Factors" (hidden patterns) in what you watch.
By keeping only the largest "Singular Values," Al ignores the random junk and focuses on the patterns that define
your taste.

Probability and
Statistics
Presented by Ms.Sayali Mane

What is a Random Variable?
A Random Variable (X) is like a machine that turns a chance event into a number.
Example: Flipping a coin!
Math works better with numbers than words!

Continuous (Measurable)
Things you measure on a continuous scale. Can take any decimal value.
Examples:
●
Time it takes to run a 100m race
●
Student height in centimeters
●
Temperature outside during the day

Discrete (Countable)
Things you can count in distinct steps (1, 2, 3...). There are no middle values.
Examples:
●
Number of goals in a soccer game
●
Number of heads in 5 coin ﬂips
●
Number of students in a classroom

Probability Distributions
A Probability Distribution lists all possible outcomes and how likely each one is to occur.
●
Rule 1: Every probability is between 0% and 100% (0 and 1).
●
Rule 2: All probabilities for all outcomes MUST add up to 100% (1.0).

Expected Value (The Average)
The Expected Value is what you expect to get on average if you repeat an experiment
many times.
E(X)=∑x⋅P(X=x)

Random Sampling
Population vs Sample
The Soup Spoon Analogy
Population: The entire giant pot of soup you are cooking.
Sample: Just one spoon of soup you taste to test the flavor.
If you stir the pot well (random sampling), one spoon gives you an accurate taste of the whole pot!

Simple Random
Pulling names out of a hat! Everyone in the population has an equal chance of being picked.
Stratified
Divide into subgroups (e.g. Grades 9, 10, 11) and randomly pick a few students from each group.
Cluster
Pick whole intact groups randomly (e.g. select 3 entire homerooms) and survey everyone inside them.

Sample Size (n): How many people or items you survey.Larger samples give more trustworthy
answers!
Sampling Bias : Unfair picking that favors one outcome over others.Always use random picking to
keep things fair.
Central Limit Theorem : Sample averages tend to form a smooth bell curve.Works great whenever
your sample size n ≥ 30!

Deep Blue (introduced by IBM) who became famous in 1997 when he defeated the Chess champion - Gary
Kasparov.
For each 3-min move, Deep Blue could analyze 50 billion positions & take a decision based on pre-programmed
software rules. This was an example of AI without ML.
Two decades passed by and the spotlight shifts to Seoul in 2016 where an even more interesting character named
AlphaGo created by Google defeated the Go world champion - Lee Sedol. This was an example of AI with ML.

AI without ML - Humans provide the rules to the machines
AI with ML - Humans provide only the data. The machines learn the rules themselves.

AI began in 1953 when Claude Shanon at Bell labs hired two assistants named
Marvin Minsky and John McCarthy
Turing had a couple of years back proposed his now-famous Turing test - ‘a
computer can be said to be intelligent if a human judge can't tell whether he is
interacting with a human or a machine’ .
Formally titled 'Artificial Intelligence'.

While John McCarthy gave the general definition of AI as “the science &
engineering of making intelligent machines or machines that think the way
humans think”,
Arthur Samuel in 1959 defined Machine Learning (ML) as - “a field of study that
gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed”.

Machine Learning
Instead of finding solution of a problem instance by following strictly defined steps of an
algorithm which is specific to the problem, they use a general algorithm with many parameters
that have to be set accordingly to the actual problem.
And these parameters are derived by a repetitive process of “learning” from samples of the
problem instances.

In AI and Machine Learning, t-distribution, F-distribution, and Chi-square
distribution are not directly used to train models like Neural Networks or Decision
Trees.
Instead, they are used for statistical analysis, feature selection, model evaluation,
hypothesis testing, and validating machine learning results.

t-distribution
The t-distribution is used when:
●
Sample size is small
●
Population variance is unknown
●
Comparing means
t-test is a statistical tool used to check if the average of two sets of data are
significantly different from each other, or if any observed difference is just random
noise.

3 Main Types of T-Tests
●
One-Sample t-test
Compare 1 sample mean against a known fixed value
Is the average height of a class different from the national average of 5 ft 9 in?
●
Independent Samples t-test
Compare means of 2 completely separate groups
Do students who study with music score differently than students who study in silence?

t-test is a statistical tool used to check if the average of two sets of data are

noise.

3 Main Types of T-Tests
●
One-Sample t-test
Compare 1 sample mean against a known fixed value
Is the average height of a class different from the national average of 5 ft 9 in?
●
Independent Samples t-test
Compare means of 2 completely separate groups
Do students who study with music score differently than students who study in silence?

●
Paired Samples t-test
Compare means from the same group at two different times.
Are patients' blood pressure levels lower after taking medication compared to before?
For a t-test to give reliable results:
●
The data should be normally distributed
●
The data points must be independent of each other.
●
Samples should ideally be continuous measurements (e.g., test scores, weights, time).

Applications:
Compare accuracy of two ML models.
To determine whether the performance difference between two machine learning models is statistically
significant.
Test significance of regression coefficients.
To determine whether an input feature has a significant effect on the target variable.
A/B testing.
To compare two versions of a product, website, or algorithm.

Example
Two image-classification models are tested on 5 datasets.
Dataset CNN ViT
1 92 90
2 91 89
3 94 91
4 90 88
5 93 91
A paired t-test checks whether CNN's higher accuracy is statistically significant.
If p < 0.05, the improvement is considered significant.

F-Distribution
Used in ANOVA to compare three or more group means and evaluate the overall significance of
regression models.
Non-Negative (F≥0): Since variance is calculated by squaring values, an F-statistic can never be
negative.
Two Sets of Degrees of Freedom: The exact shape of the curve depends on two parameters:
1.
Numerator degrees of freedom (df1): Based on the sample size/groups in the top variance.
2.
Denominator degrees of freedom (df2): Based on the sample size/groups in the bottom variance.

F-Distribution
Applications:
• Compare multiple ML algorithms.
• Numerical feature selection (ANOVA F-test).
• Evaluate regression models.

Example
Suppose four models produce the following accuracies:
Random Forest = 94%
SVM = 92%
XGBoost = 96%
Neural Network = 97%
Instead of performing many t-tests, ANOVA uses the F-statistic to determine whether at least one model performs
significantly better.

Chi-Square Distribution
Used with categorical variables to test independence and perform feature
selection.
Applications:
• Select important categorical features.
• Spam filtering.
• Customer analytics.

Example
Online shopping dataset:
Gender Purchased Not Purchased
Male 120 80
Female 90 110
A Chi-square test determines whether purchasing behaviour depends on gender. A
significant result means gender and purchasing are associated.

Customer churn refers to customers who stop using a company's product or service.
Companies such as telecom providers, banks, insurance companies, and streaming
platforms use AI and Machine Learning to predict which customers are likely to
leave.

Real-world Example: Customer Churn Prediction
Features: Age, Monthly Charges, Contract Type, Internet Service.
• t-test: Compare average monthly charges of customers who stayed vs. left.
• F-test: Compare average charges across Monthly, 1-Year and 2-Year contracts.
• Chi-square: Test whether Contract Type is associated with customer churn.

Sampling from a Bivariate Normal
Distribution
A bivariate normal distribution is a probability distribution involving two related continuous variables
(X and Y) that are both normally distributed.
Example:
●
X = Height of students
●
Y = Weight of students
Since height and weight are related, they can be modeled using a bivariate normal distribution.

For Example :
Variable X : Height , Age
Variable Y : Weight , Salary
A bivariate normal distribution tracks two variables at the same time where:
1.
Each variable individually follows a normal bell curve.
2.
They are connected by correlation

A normal distribution is perfectly symmetrical, meaning a vertical line drawn through the center of the
curve divides it into two identical mirror images.
Because of this perfect symmetry, the measures of central tendency, the mean, the median (middle value),
and the mode (most frequent value), all fall at the exact same point in the center of the distribution.

●
Generate random pairs of values (X, Y).
●
Observe how the two variables change together.
●
Verify that the generated data follows the specified mean, variance, and
correlation.

Government of India - Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation (MoSPI)
National Sample Survey (NSS) Manual on Sampling Methodology
Section 1: Sampling Design and Stratified Sampling
The National Sample Survey adopts a multi-stage stratified sampling design for nationwide
socio-economic inquiries. The first stage units (FSUs) are census villages in the rural sector and Urban
Frame Survey (UFS) blocks in urban areas. Stratification is carried out by grouping districts with
similar agricultural, economic, and demographic characteristics.
Proportional allocation of sample size across strata ensures that the variance of observations is
minimized effectively. Within each rural stratum, villages are selected with Probability Proportional to
Size with Replacement (PPSWR). In urban strata, simple random sampling without replacement
(SRSWOR) is adopted for selecting sample blocks. Each stratum is treated as an independent
population domain to guarantee representative statistical precision across India.

Section 2: Estimation Procedure, Multipliers and Mathematical Formulation
For estimating population aggregates, estimation formulas and sampling weights (multipliers) are
strictly applied by survey supervisors. Let y_hij denote the observed value of characteristic y for the
j-th sample household in the i-th FSU of the h-th stratum.
The base multiplier formula W_h is given by W_h = N_h / n_h, where N_h is the total number of FSUs
in stratum h and n_h is the sample size. Sample weights ensure unbiased estimation of totals,
averages, ratios, and standard errors for official planning. Sub-sample estimates are computed
independently to generate valid estimates of standard error and sampling variance across rounds.

Section 3: Cluster Sampling and Secondary Stage Selection
Cluster sampling is implemented when hamlet-groups or sub-blocks are formed in large villages to
control field investigator workload. In cluster sampling, clusters of contiguous households are listed,
and two or more clusters are chosen at random without bias.
Ultimate stage units (USUs) are households selected through systematic sampling from each listing
block. Non-sampling errors are monitored through standardized field re-interviews and rigorous data
validation protocols.

MedAssist-AI
Disease Prediction Model Development, Optimization, and System Integration
Sanvi Sawant

CHAPTER 1
PROJECT DESCRIPTION
1.1 Introduction
During Milestone 3 of the MedAssist AI project, my primary responsibility was the
development, optimization, and evaluation of the machine learning pipeline for disease
prediction. I worked extensively on preparing the medical dataset by performing data
preprocessing, exploratory data analysis, identifying class imbalance, implementing
downsampling techniques, training multiple machine learning models, and optimizing their
performance through hyperparameter tuning. I also evaluated each model using multiple
performance metrics to determine the most suitable approach for disease prediction.
In addition to the machine learning pipeline, I was responsible for the complete integration of
the application. This involved integrating the React (Vite) frontend, FastAPI backend,
authentication module, analytics dashboard, reporting system, and machine learning
prediction engine into a single unified application. I configured API communication between
all modules, integrated the trained Voting Classifier model with the backend, ensured correct
preprocessing and disease mapping during inference, implemented secure session
management, and verified role-based access for both patients and doctors.
The objective of my work was to develop a reliable disease prediction pipeline while
ensuring seamless communication between every component of the MedAssist AI platform.
The final integrated system was validated through end-to-end testing by verifying API
endpoints, model loading, dataset integrity, prediction workflows, and overall application
stability, resulting in a fully functional healthcare platform ready for deployment and
demonstration.
1.2 Objectives
The objectives of my work during Milestone 3 were as follows:
●​ To perform detailed exploratory data analysis on the medical dataset and understand its
characteristics.
●​ To preprocess the dataset by cleaning the data, encoding disease labels, and preparing it
for machine learning.
●​ To identify and analyze class imbalance within the dataset and implement suitable
techniques to improve model performance.
●​ To train and evaluate multiple machine learning models, for disease prediction.
●​ To perform hyperparameter tuning to improve the accuracy, robustness, and generalization
capability of the trained models.
●​ To compare model performance using evaluation metrics such as Accuracy, Precision,
Recall, F1-Score, Macro F1-Score, and Top-3 Accuracy.
●​ To contribute to the ensemble learning approach used in the final disease prediction
system.
●​ To integrate the complete application by connecting the React frontend, FastAPI backend,
authentication system, analytics module, reporting module, and machine learning pipeline.
●​ To validate the complete system through end-to-end testing, ensuring reliable
communication between all components and successful prediction generation.

CHAPTER 2
DATASET DESCRIPTION
2.1 Overview of the Dataset
During the previous milestones, the machine learning models developed for disease
prediction achieved lower-than-expected accuracy. To improve the overall performance of the
system, my primary objective during Milestone 3 was to investigate the factors affecting
model accuracy and identify suitable optimization techniques. The first step in this process
was a detailed analysis of the dataset used for disease prediction.
The dataset consisted of patient symptoms as input features and their corresponding diseases
as the target variable, making it a multi-class classification problem. I began by exploring the
dataset to understand its structure, quality, and distribution before proceeding with model
development. Since machine learning models are highly dependent on the quality and
distribution of the training data, this analysis was essential for identifying potential issues that
could be affecting prediction performance.
During this analysis, I discovered that the primary challenge was the highly imbalanced
distribution of disease classes. While a few diseases contained thousands of samples, many
diseases had only a limited number of observations. This imbalance caused the models
trained in the earlier milestones to become biased towards majority classes, resulting in lower
overall performance and poor prediction of rare diseases. This finding formed the foundation

CHAPTER 3
DATA PREPROCESSING
Data preprocessing is a critical phase in the machine learning pipeline that involves
transforming raw medical data into a clean, structured, and representative format suitable for
model training. This stage addresses various data quality issues, such as missing values and
inconsistencies, while also preparing the feature set and target variables for effective learning.
The following sections detail the specific preprocessing steps implemented to optimize the
performance of the MedAssist AI prediction engine.

3.1 Dataset Cleaning
The first preprocessing step involved verifying the quality of the dataset. I inspected the
dataset for missing values, duplicate records, incorrect data types, and inconsistencies that
could negatively affect model training.
The analysis showed that the dataset was generally well-structured and did not contain
significant missing values or duplicate records requiring removal. Nevertheless, verifying
these aspects was an important step because even a small number of inconsistent records can
reduce model reliability and introduce unnecessary bias during training.
I also verified that all symptom features were correctly represented and that the target
variable contained valid encoded disease labels before proceeding with further preprocessing.
3.2 Dataset Preparation
After completing the initial preprocessing steps, I prepared the dataset for machine learning
by separating the symptom features from the target disease labels. The symptom columns
were used as the input features (X), while the encoded disease labels formed the target
variable (y). This separation enabled the machine learning models to learn the relationship
between different symptom combinations and their corresponding diseases.
To ensure that the model evaluation remained reliable and representative of the overall
dataset, I performed a stratified train-test split. Stratification preserved the original
distribution of disease classes in both the training and testing datasets, preventing majority
classes from dominating either split and ensuring that minority disease classes were also
represented during evaluation.
Following the dataset split, I conducted a detailed analysis of the disease distribution within
the test dataset. This analysis helped identify rare diseases, defined as diseases having three
or fewer samples in the testing set. Since overall accuracy alone does not adequately measure
performance on highly imbalanced datasets, I specifically evaluated the model's ability to
predict these rare diseases using additional performance metrics such as Macro F1-Score,
Top-3 Accuracy, and average precision, recall, and F1-score for rare disease classes. This
provided a more comprehensive assessment of the model's performance across both common
and infrequent diseases.
3.3 Analysis of Class Imbalance
After preparing the dataset for model training, I conducted a detailed analysis of the disease
distribution to understand the reason behind the lower prediction accuracies obtained during
the previous milestones. Although the dataset was complete and properly structured, I
observed that the number of samples available for each disease varied significantly. A small
number of diseases contained thousands of training samples, while many diseases had only a
limited number of observations.
This uneven distribution indicated the presence of class imbalance, a common challenge in
multi-class classification problems. During model training, machine learning algorithms tend
to learn more effectively from classes with a larger number of samples, while classes with
very few observations receive comparatively less importance. As a result, the models become

biased toward majority disease classes and struggle to correctly predict rare diseases, even if
the overall accuracy appears satisfactory.
To better understand the severity of this imbalance, I analyzed the frequency of each disease
class and categorized diseases based on the number of available samples. The analysis
confirmed that several diseases contained only a handful of observations, making them
difficult for the models to learn effectively. This explained the comparatively lower
accuracies achieved during earlier milestones and indicated that improving the dataset
representation was more important than simply changing machine learning algorithms.
Since overall accuracy alone could not accurately reflect the model's ability to predict
minority disease classes, I decided to include additional evaluation metrics such as Macro
F1-Score, Top-3 Accuracy, and separate performance analysis for rare diseases. These
metrics provided a more balanced evaluation by considering the performance of both
majority and minority classes, enabling a more reliable assessment of model performance.
The findings from this analysis formed the basis for the preprocessing and optimization
strategies implemented in the subsequent stages of this milestone, including downsampling
experiments, hyperparameter tuning, and ensemble learning.
3.4 Handling Single-Sample Classes
To address the technical limitations of stratified splitting for classes with only one sample, I
ensured these specific instances remained within the training set, allowing the model to learn
from them without causing split-time errors.
During the preprocessing stage, I observed that a few disease classes contained only a single
sample in the entire dataset. Performing a stratified train-test split on such classes is not
possible because stratification requires at least one sample to be present in both the training
and testing datasets.
To address this issue, I identified all disease classes containing only one sample and ensured
that these samples remained exclusively within the training dataset. This approach prevented
errors during dataset splitting while still allowing the machine learning models to learn from
these rare disease classes during training.
The remaining disease classes, which contained sufficient samples, were then used for
stratified train-test splitting. This preprocessing step ensured that the dataset could be divided
successfully while preserving the class distribution of all eligible disease categories.
3.5 Stratified Train-Test Split
After handling the single-sample disease classes, I divided the remaining dataset into training
and testing sets using a stratified 80:20 train-test split. Stratification ensured that the
distribution of disease classes remained approximately consistent across both datasets,
allowing the machine learning models to be trained and evaluated on representative data.
The training dataset was used for learning the relationship between symptoms and diseases,
while the testing dataset was reserved for evaluating model performance on previously

unseen samples. Maintaining separate datasets helped assess the generalization capability of
the trained models and reduced the risk of overfitting.
CHAPTER 4

4.1 Selection of Machine Learning Models
As part of my contribution during Milestone 3, I was responsible for developing and
evaluating multiple machine learning models for disease prediction. Initially, four ensemble
learning algorithms I selected for experimentation: Random Forest, XGBoost, Gradient
Boosting, and LightGBM. These algorithms were chosen because they perform well on
structured tabular datasets and are capable of handling multi-class classification problems
efficiently.
Each model was trained independently using the preprocessed dataset and subsequently
optimized through hyperparameter tuning to improve prediction performance. The objective
was to compare the strengths and limitations of each algorithm and identify the models that
achieved the best balance between accuracy, robustness, and generalization.
After evaluating the performance of all four models, Random Forest, XGBoost, and
LightGBM demonstrated the most suitable performance for ensemble learning and were
therefore selected for the final Voting Classifier implemented in the complete MedAssist AI
system. Although Gradient Boosting was trained and evaluated as part of my work, it was not
included in the final ensemble because the selected combination of models produced better
overall performance.

4.2 Random Forest Model
The first model I developed during Milestone 3 was the Random Forest Classifier. Since
Random Forest is an ensemble learning algorithm that combines the predictions of multiple
decision trees using the bagging technique, it was selected as the baseline model for the
disease prediction task. Its ability to handle high-dimensional tabular datasets and reduce
overfitting made it an appropriate starting point for experimentation.
I initially trained the model using its default configuration to establish a baseline
performance. After analysing the results, multiple experiments were conducted by modifying
important hyperparameters such as the number of decision trees, maximum tree depth,
minimum samples required for node splitting, and class weighting strategy. Different
combinations of these parameters were evaluated to improve the model's ability to generalize
across both majority and minority disease classes.
The optimized Random Forest model demonstrated a significant improvement over the
baseline configuration and served as one of the strongest individual models developed during
this milestone. Owing to its consistent performance and robustness, it was later selected as
one of the constituent models for the final Voting Classifier.
4.3 XGBoost Model
The second model developed during this milestone was Extreme Gradient Boosting
(XGBoost). XGBoost is a gradient boosting algorithm that builds decision trees sequentially,
where each new tree attempts to correct the prediction errors of the previous trees. Its
regularization capabilities and efficient optimization techniques make it one of the most
widely used algorithms for structured machine learning datasets.
The model was initially trained using default parameters and subsequently optimized through
several experimental iterations. Hyperparameters such as the learning rate, maximum tree
depth, number of estimators, and subsampling parameters were adjusted to improve
prediction performance while reducing overfitting. The impact of each parameter change was
analysed by comparing the resulting evaluation metrics.
Among all the individual models trained during this milestone, XGBoost consistently
achieved one of the highest prediction accuracies and demonstrated strong generalization
capability. Due to its superior performance, it became one of the primary models selected for
the final ensemble learning approach.

4.4 Gradient Boosting Model
The third model implemented as part of my work was the Gradient Boosting Classifier. This
algorithm builds an ensemble of weak learners sequentially, where each successive model
focuses on correcting the errors made by the previous model. Gradient Boosting was included
in the experimentation phase to compare its performance with other ensemble learning
algorithms on the disease prediction dataset.
After training the model using the preprocessed dataset, multiple parameter configurations
were evaluated to improve its predictive performance. The experiments focused on tuning
parameters such as the number of estimators, learning rate, and maximum tree depth. The
optimized model was then compared with the remaining algorithms using the selected
evaluation metrics.
Although Gradient Boosting produced satisfactory results, its overall performance was
comparatively lower than the optimized Random Forest and XGBoost models. Consequently,
while it contributed to the comparative analysis, it was not selected for inclusion in the final
Voting Classifier.
4.5 LightGBM Model
The final model developed during this milestone was LightGBM, an efficient gradient
boosting framework designed for fast training and lower memory consumption. LightGBM
was selected because of its ability to process large structured datasets efficiently while
maintaining competitive predictive performance.
During experimentation, several preprocessing adjustments were required to ensure
compatibility with LightGBM, including feature name standardization. After successfully
training the model, multiple hyperparameter combinations involving the number of
estimators, maximum tree depth, and minimum child samples were evaluated to improve
performance.
Although the individual accuracy of LightGBM was comparatively lower than that of
Random Forest and XGBoost, it learned decision boundaries differently and therefore
introduced useful diversity during ensemble learning. For this reason, it was retained as one
of the constituent models in the final Voting Classifier.
4.6 Hyperparameter Tuning
After training the initial versions of the selected machine learning models, I observed that
their default configurations did not provide the best possible performance for the disease
prediction task. To improve prediction accuracy and generalization capability, I performed
hyperparameter tuning on each model through multiple experimental iterations.
The tuning process involved modifying important model parameters and analysing their
impact on the evaluation metrics. Rather than relying on a single configuration, several
parameter combinations were tested for each algorithm to determine the most suitable
settings for the given dataset. The objective was to improve model performance while
minimizing overfitting and ensuring consistent predictions across different disease classes.

The parameters adjusted during experimentation included the number of estimators,
maximum tree depth, learning rate, minimum samples required for node splitting, minimum
child samples, and other model-specific parameters. Each experiment was evaluated using the
predefined performance metrics, and the configuration producing the most balanced results
was selected as the final model configuration.
The optimized models obtained through this tuning process were subsequently used for
comparative performance analysis and later contributed to the development of the final
ensemble Voting Classifier.

Following the completion of model training and hyperparameter tuning, I compared the

CHAPTER 5

5.1 Evaluation Metrics
To evaluate the effectiveness of the trained machine learning models, I used multiple
evaluation metrics instead of relying solely on overall accuracy. Since the disease prediction
problem involved a large number of disease classes with an imbalanced distribution, a single
metric could not completely represent model performance. Therefore, several complementary
metrics were selected to assess the models from different perspectives.
Accuracy was used to measure the overall percentage of correctly classified disease
instances. Precision measured the correctness of positive predictions, while Recall evaluated
the model's ability to identify the actual disease classes. The F1-Score provided a balanced
measure by considering both Precision and Recall simultaneously.
In addition to these conventional metrics, Macro F1-Score was used to evaluate the
performance of each disease class equally, regardless of the number of available samples.
Top-3 Accuracy was also calculated to determine whether the correct disease appeared
among the top three predicted diseases. Furthermore, a separate evaluation was performed on
rare diseases to analyse the model's capability to predict diseases having very limited testing
samples.

Government of India - Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation (MoSPI)
National Sample Survey (NSS) Manual on Sampling Methodology
Section 1: Sampling Design and Stratified Sampling
The National Sample Survey adopts a multi-stage stratified sampling design for nationwide
socio-economic inquiries. The first stage units (FSUs) are census villages in the rural sector and Urban
Frame Survey (UFS) blocks in urban areas. Stratification is carried out by grouping districts with
similar agricultural, economic, and demographic characteristics.
Proportional allocation of sample size across strata ensures that the variance of observations is
minimized effectively. Within each rural stratum, villages are selected with Probability Proportional to
Size with Replacement (PPSWR). In urban strata, simple random sampling without replacement
(SRSWOR) is adopted for selecting sample blocks. Each stratum is treated as an independent
population domain to guarantee representative statistical precision across India.

Section 2: Estimation Procedure, Multipliers and Mathematical Formulation
For estimating population aggregates, estimation formulas and sampling weights (multipliers) are
strictly applied by survey supervisors. Let y_hij denote the observed value of characteristic y for the
j-th sample household in the i-th FSU of the h-th stratum.
The base multiplier formula W_h is given by W_h = N_h / n_h, where N_h is the total number of FSUs
in stratum h and n_h is the sample size. Sample weights ensure unbiased estimation of totals,
averages, ratios, and standard errors for official planning. Sub-sample estimates are computed
independently to generate valid estimates of standard error and sampling variance across rounds.

Section 3: Cluster Sampling and Secondary Stage Selection
Cluster sampling is implemented when hamlet-groups or sub-blocks are formed in large villages to
control field investigator workload. In cluster sampling, clusters of contiguous households are listed,
and two or more clusters are chosen at random without bias.
Ultimate stage units (USUs) are households selected through systematic sampling from each listing
block. Non-sampling errors are monitored through standardized field re-interviews and rigorous data
validation protocols.
